newsitem.title: USA: Thomson unveils DVD, keeps expectations low.
newsitem.headline: Thomson unveils DVD, keeps expectations low.

text.p: Thomson Consumer Electronics, a unit of giant French electronics maker Thomson SA, has unveiled its line of new digital video disk (DVD) players, but company officials are keeping initial sales expectations low.
DVD is the new format for playing movies on television, much like videocassette recorders. DVD's digital signals, however, provide a clearer picture and crisper audio than analog-based videotape.
Moreover the movies, which are played on disks the size and shape of audio CDs, can show movies in different languages, with subtitles, and in both film screen and TV screen size.

At a news conference here on Thursday, Thomson spotlighted three DVD players starting with the RCA RC5200 at a suggested price of $499, which is down from a planned $599 and equal to rival Toshiba Corp.'s least expensive player.
Two advanced models, the RCA RC5500 and ProScan brand PS8600, have suggested prices of $699 and $749, respectively.

Thomson began shipping players to seven key markets in March, and it will have products on retail shelves in other markets when movie titles become available in those markets, Larry Pesce, manager of DVD product management, said in an interview.
"The 1995 DVD launch (for RCA) is finally here," Pesce said, alluding to well over a year of delays in the product launch while copyright and security issues were solved.

Four of Hollywood's studios, Walt Disney Co., Universal Inc., a unit of Seagram Co. Ltd., Paramount, owned by Viacom Inc. and News Corp.'s Fox have withheld support due to concern about digital piracy. Also, they are waiting to see how the DVD market develops before committing fully to it.

Warner Bros. and New Line Cinema, units of Time Warner Inc., Metro Goldwyn Mayer Inc., Columbia Pictures, a division of Sony Corp., Philips Electronics NV's Polygram and laser disc maker Image Entertainment Inc. all support DVD.
The divided film industry and delayed launch have kept some consumer electronics manufacturers decidedly downbeat about DVD sales in 1997.
"My expectations are not that you'll see a phenomenal success in the first six months," Pesce said about sales of the players.

The low-key attitude is a direct contrast to late 1995 and early 1996 when DVD was seen as holding the key for future sales growth in the industry because it was the first product that merged digital home entertainment with computer applications.

Thomson expects 350,000 to 400,000 DVD players to be sold this year bsaed on pent-up demand for the high-tech product, and Pesce said the company traditionally captures 25 percent of any new market it enters.
Sales in 1998 are expected to pick up from consumers who are more technologically savvy, but who are waiting for lower cost machines and slightly advanced features.
"Our best guess is that group will buy (DVD) next year," he said, adding forecasts call for as many as 1.8 million DVD player sales in 1998.
Along with its players, Thomson is offering a pre-packaged display of 24 movie titles in the DVD format to be sold alongside DVD players.
Thomson's seven initial markets for the DVD roll-out are New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, San Francisco, Washington D.C., Seattle and Dallas.
